messages.body_plain:
Hi listfolks,

New versions of the Distance and mrds R packages are now available on
CRAN. I've attached the release notes below. These two releases fix a
number of bugs, many of which were first reported on this list. Thanks
to all those who have taken the time to contact us and help out by
reporting unusual behaviour or requesting features.

You should be able to obtain new versions by simply running
update.packages() in R.

All the best,
--dave

---

Release notes:

Distance 1.0.1
----------------------

* fix bug in dht2 when object IDs were not specified in flatfile
formatted data
* fix bugs in bootdht where the function crashed if all models failed to
fit and when the hessian couldn't be computed
* better checking of data$observer, thanks to Martin Biuw for pointing
this out
* fix bug in dht2 where the covered area was calculated incorrectly when
left truncation was used for point transects
* add example data for camera trap distance sampling, see
?DuikerCameraTrap for more information
* Stratum area column (Area) is no longer required by ds(). If it is
omitted density estimates are returned.
* Fix bug when dht2 is used with pre-binned data. Thanks to Delphine
Ducros for reporting this bug.
* Fix to dht2 bugs when Innes et al estimator is used for encounter rate
variance estimation
* fix bootdht issue where convert.units argument was not handled properly

mrds 2.2.3
----------

* fix bug where region areas were not duplicated properly when density
was estimated (using Area=0 in data)
* fix a bug in getting starting values for hazard-rate detection
functions when point transect data is used
* fix issue with left truncation when estimating abundance/density in dht

messages.body_plain:
Samrat

Good for you to be conscious of distance sampling assumptions prior to data collection.  The method you describe is one way to estimate g(0) (probability of detecting animals on the transect).  It requires that you are able to recognise which of your detections are duplicates; you will need to decide if the 20 minutes elapsed between visits will permit identifying the duplicates.  An additional concern is whether animals will remain stationary over that period of time (perhaps the "slow" loris will adhere to remaining in place, I cannot say for the flying squirrels).

As a sort of pilot study, before launching the full double observer team survey, can you estimate the value of g(0) from a set of trials whereby observers travel down transects where squirrels/loris are known to be present on the transect.  Record the number of observers that do and do not detect the animals present on the track.  That can provide a first approximation regarding the magnitude of the g(0)=1 assumption violation.

messages.subject_clean: DSM estimating over-abundance
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am running DSM for two season data (Summer and Winter) for ungulate species. Detection function is estimating higher detection probability in Summer probably due to larger cluster size and increased visibility. When moving forward with this to spatial abundance estimation using DSM, it is highly over-estimating the abundances.
Model parameters were then corrected for influential observations, smoothers wiggliness. Model details are the following:

Summary of uncertainty in a density surface model calculated
 analytically for GAM, with delta method
Approximate asymptotic confidence interval:
       2.5%        Mean       97.5%
   66298.34  2098572.22 66427079.21
(Using log-Normal approximation)

Point estimate                 : 2098572
CV of detection function       : 0.1115305
CV from GAM                    : 4.62
Total standard error           : 9698296
Total coefficient of variation : 4.6214

I figured out a few probable causes for this:
1. larger cluster size variation in Summer (correction for this did not help much)
2. High detection probability
3. Model is predicting high abundance in the non-sampled area that have similar covariate values as those segments where sightings have occurred.

I do not understand what else could cause this and how to correct this?
I would be more than happy to share more details on this.

Many Thanks and Regards,
Deepti Gupta

Sounds as if you may have extrapolation issues arising from unusual covariate combinations in some of your non-sampled grid cells.  Could be the case that a small number of grid cells are contributing to the massive abundance estimates.

Bouchet , P J-F , Miller , D L , Roberts , J , Mannocci , L , Harris , C M & Thomas , L 2019 , From here and now to there and then : practical recommendations for extrapolating cetacean density surface models to novel conditions . CREEM Technical Report , no. 2019-1 , University of St Andrews .

available online at https://research-repository.st-andrews.ac.uk/handle/10023/18509

This may help isolate some of your problems.

messages.subject_clean: How to estimate the density and abundance of tree species along an elevation gradient with distance sampling
messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

I am a little lost with the analyses I need to carry out in order to understand how the density /abundance of several species of trees changes with elevation and other variables I collected. Maybe somebody can offer some guidance on which methods, R packages , literature or manuals that could be useful.

Context: I want to understand how elevation and light availability interact and shape the distribution of several tree species.

Data: I have 24 line transects along an elevation gradient where each transect is perpendicular to the elevation gradient (each transect is located at a single elevation). I collected info about each of the individuals of the target species in the transect (perpendicular distance to the transect, diameter, basal area around the individual, tree height, light availability, slope...). I also have information of some of this variables at different subtransects, within each transect.

Main Idea: 1) I want to correct/adjust the observed abundances along the transect with a detection probability model.
                  2) use gams to understand if the interaction between elevation and light availability affects the adjusted abundance/density of the species. To answer the          main question of the study I do not need to extrapolate to areas where I do not have any observation.

What I have done so far: I was able to fit several detection probability models with different covariates. Also, I have used dsm to build a model to understand how the interaction between elevation and light availability influence the adjusted counts. After that, to visualize the results of the model, I have predicted the adjusted counts along the elevation gradient. These predictions follow in a way the observed patterns, however the abundance estimations are really biased.  I am more interested in the patterns along the elevation gradient, rather than accurate estimations of abundance or density.

Questions: 1) Is dsm the "best" approach?
                   2) As I have the information about the covariates for both the detection and abundance at the individual level, I think I don't need to cluster the observations.
                      Does this make the Effort in dsm equivalent to 1 (the distance and length of the transect and subtransect is measured in meters)? I also thought that the Effort           could be the distance between each individual... however using effort = 1 or effort = to the distance between observations gives very different results...
                   3) When predicting, I am not sure what will be the offset of my dataset...

I am probably doing many things wrong. So far, I have spent already quite some time reading and trying to find examples to follow unsuccessfully. Thus, I would appreciate any reference or guidance on how to work with distance sampling estimations along gradients (gradients in abundance?) where there is a potential interaction between several of the variables that determine the abundances.

Thanks a lot!

Miguel Muñoz Mazón

messages.subject_clean: [distance-sampling] How to estimate the density and abundance of tree species along an elevation gradient with distance sampling
messages.body_plain:
Hi Miguel,

I'll have a go at answering - perhaps others will have different opinions.

I'll start by assuming that your 24 transects, each at a unique
elevation, represent a sample size of 24 for examining the relationship
between plan density (response variable) and elevation and light
availability (explanatory variables).  I'll assume elevation is known
for each transect.  I'll assume that light availability is also known,
although in practice you would use the mean of the light availability
measured at each observed plant on a transect, which is an estimate not
a known quantity (see later).

Regarding your questions:

(1) Given the above, you can use the dsm package to do the analysis,
with transect as the unit of analysis for the density surface model; you
could use standard model selection methods to tell you whether
elevation, light availability as main effects, or these plus the
interaction between elevation and light availability, is the most
parsimonious model.

(2) I think the unit of analysis here is the transect.  It does not make
sense (to me) to talk about "density" at the individual plant level.  It
also may not make sense to work at the "subtransect" level but see below
for more on this.

Effort is the line length for each transect.

(3) As with all dsm models this is dependent on what you use for the
response variable, and it is set automatically by the dsm function.
Perhaps I am mis-understanding you.

I do not understand why your predicted density estimates appear biased.
Perhaps we can correspond off the list about this, and any other
questions you have, and then post a summary back to the list?

Regarding the use of subtransects, I can see an argument for working at
the subtransect level rather than the transect level, if average light
availability varies substantially between sections of transect.
However, in this case, you'll need to be careful to check for residual
correlation between subtransects, after the modelling is done, otherwise
you'll be guilty of pseudoreplication because the response variable will
not be independent given the covariates between subtransects.

I hope this is helpful; I'm sure other analysis approaches are possible!

Best wishes, Len Thomas

messages.body_plain:
Hi Miguel, hi listfolk,

Just a couple of things to follow-up on here from Len's message,
apologies for re-iterating some of his points.

First off a boiler plate warning that DSMs are not a method for causal
inference, so statements you make about the model results are only
really going to be in terms of "altitude and abundance are correlated in
this way". Direct biological interpretation of resulting smooths is
conditional on getting the model right, so it's a bit dicey.

I'm finding it a bit difficult to get my head around the exact setup
here when it comes to what the sample unit should be. An important
question I think is whether light availability is only a function of
altitude or whether it varies with aspect (or if there is enough
variation with aspect along the transect for light availability to
change). If light availability changes along the transect, then I think
you need to chop up the segments, if it doesn't vary then you haven't
lost any information by averaging at the transect level. That being
said, if the light level only changes with altitude, then it's not clear
that you need both in the model? (I think I'm assuming that your
transects are all on the same side of the same hill, but that might not
be true!)

If you have the segmented model, then you can probably fit a model like

count ~ ti(altitude) + ti(light) + ti(altitude, light)

this construction allows you to decompose the interaction between the
variables, so you can investigate what's going on (it's equivalent to
using the tensor product te() but with the bonus you can see what each
term is doing). Carrying on from the issue of getting the model right,
you might want to include smooths of other covariates that you think
influence abundance in this model, else you might end up with spurious
effects.

The effort should be the transect/segment line length for each sample
unit. So if transect 1 is 1km long, it would be 1000m, say (if your
detection distances are in metres and you want to keep everything in
consistent units).

I'm curious about what you mean by "biased" results for abundance. Feel
free to contact me off-list about that.

The offset for predictions correspond to the area you are predicting
over. In your case, you're not so interested in making abundance
predictions but more the shape of the resulting smooths. In that case
you could set the offset to 1 and just compare densities? Making
predictions for altitude-light combinations could give you something
like this plot http://converged.yt/talks/dsm-csiro/talk.html#/45 (note
that plot is on the log scale) where you can (qualitatively) assess
"hotspots" in covariate space. You may also want to marginalise over
light availability and just look at the average altitude effect?

At the risk of self-promotion, I was involved in a paper using distance
sampling and specifically DSMs for oak trees with collaborators in
Portugal, which might be useful for you:

Dias, FS, DL Miller, TA Marques, J Marcelino, MC Caldeira, JO Cerdeira,
MN Bugalho (2016). Conservation zones promote oak regeneration and shrub
diversity in certified Mediterranean oak woodlands. Biological
Conservation 195, 226-234.

Preprint at http://converged.yt/papers/dias-2016-manuscript.pdf (happy
to send anyone the final copy if you e-mail me).

Feel free to contact me off-list to follow-up on any of these points and
we can post a summary back to folks here.

All the best,
--dave

messages.body_plain:
Hello my name is Jeff.
I'm new to distance sampling but grateful to have found this resource.

I am working with an older shipboard seabird survey dataset where behavior was recorded. The radial distances were recorded in bins out to 300 m. I noticed that the data is zero-inflated and upon further investigation the high number of counts on the line are primarily driven by birds that were assigned the behavior "directional flight" (15% of birds in this behavior category have a perpendicular distance of zero). Binning the data does not alleviate the zero-inflation.

I suspect that in-flight birds were observed approaching the line from the non-survey side of the ship and recorded as they passed the line and through the survey area, causing an increase in zeros - The majority of radial distances are in the 200-300m and the majority of angles are zero. When I constrain the analysis to only include birds with the behavior of "sitting", "foraging", and "circling" the detection function is far more reasonable. But now of course I'm ignoring the birds in directional flight. For the purposes of relative abundance across the area this isn't such a bad thing but I'd like to correct for birds in directional flight if possible.

I came across a passage in the Buckland et al. 2015 (sec 10.2.1)

"Another solution to birds in flight is to survey only birds on the sea, then separately estimate the proportion of time spent flying, so that the abundance estimate can be adjusted for flying birds." This is a good solution but I'm afraid I don't have the accompanying data to inform this.

Has anyone experienced this issue before - or have any ideas about incorporating these directional flight birds into abundance estimates? Or perhaps treating the bird in directional flight as a totally separate analysis?

Sincerely grateful for your time and thoughts,

Jeff

Hmm - worked fine for me (attached code), although I had to remove
column 21 from the dataset in the call to ds() because "observer" is a
reserved word and I got an error message with it in.  If the same code
produces different results on different machines then it's often hard to
diagnose -- but I'd start by checking carefully that the data frame in
by read.csv is exactly as you think it should be.

(I notice from the plot and gof test that the baseline hn model gave a
poor fit, with too many observations close to the point relative to what
is expected by the fitted model.  Not necessarily indicative of a
problem, since this is just a baseline model, but you may find a model
that fits well (and after truncation, etc) has quite a steep drop-off in
detectability at relatively small ranges, so you'll need to ask yourself
if this is plausible or whether there could be some problem such as
animal movement.)

Cheers, Len

messages.body_plain:
Just a thought Vaughn, but if off-road transects aren't a realistic option and you reckon that sampling routes following roads are resulting in a highly non-random distance distribution of these beasts, you might consider using the road transect counts as an index of abundance, rather than trying to convert them into actual densities. If there is a reason you need the real densities then this isn't a good option. But often people decide they need densities in situations where relative abundances might serve them just as well. For instance, if your main purpose is to compare between islands, habitats, towns etc. to identify where problems with these iguanas are worst, a good measure of relative abundance could work just as well as true densities.

If for any reason you really need true densities, you might try short transects going perpendicular to the road, to get a sense of the degree to which lizard distribution is skewed towards the road. The feasibility of this would obviously depend on your finding an adequate number of sufficiently representative points along your roads where it is possible to run perpendicular transects that are long enough to pick up the relevant variation in iguana density with distance from road.

Whatever you do, I imagine road type (width and surface) might be an important thing to control for in your analyses.

Cheers,

Mark

messages.body_plain:
Jeff

Welcome to the email list.  You indeed are working with a data set that contains some tricky bits.  Animal movement poses challenges in performing abundance estimation from distance sampling.

You also note that the survey employed one-sided transects.  This protocol is briefly mentioned in Buckland et al. (2015, Sect 10.5.2) and is something that should be avoided, because as you note, animals that appear from the "off effort" side of the ship contribute considerably to the spike in detections at distance zero, consequently resulting in a detection function that drops off rapidly, producing positive bias in the abundance estimates.

I don't have any magic solutions to this set of circumstances. Here are a couple of untested suggestions (don't think there is support in the literature for them).
If the bird flight is directional, is the flight direction recorded in the data?  If so, perhaps you could exclude birds flying from the off-effort direction.
Another situation where "spike at zero" data arises is in jungle situations where transects are cut into vegetation, resulting in detections at distance in the forward direction, but poor detection in other directions.  One possible approach in both the jungle situation as well as your situation is to invoke a "forward truncation" criterion.  Admittedly, the decision regarding that forward distance will be subjective, and open to dispute.  But given you have distance and bearing, you have the opportunity to exclude flying birds that are at distance and at small angles.

Just to round out the discussion, I presume you are aware of the 1984 paper by Tasker et al. that describes methodology dealing with shipboard seabird surveys:
Tasker, Mark L., Peter Hope Jones, Tim Dixon, and Barry F. Blake. 1984. Counting Seabirds at Sea from Ships: A Review of Methods Employed and a Suggestion for a Standardized Approach. The Auk 101 (3): 567–77. https://doi.org/10.1093/auk/101.3.567.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Jeff,

Further to Eric's final comment, are you aware that seabirds at sea surveys often employ rather different methods to survey birds first detected on the water and those first detected in flight? Birds on the water generally move slowly with respect to the survey vessel, so they can readily be analysed in a distance sampling framework. In contrast, birds in flight, generally move faster than the vessel, violating one of the assumptions of distance sampling. In short, the motion of birds relative the survey vessel results in an increase in encounter rate. Tasker et al. proposed a 'snapshot' method to deal with this (but see Gaston, Auk, 104(2): 336-338 fro limitations). In effect, this is a plot survey for birds in flight, carried out simultaneously with the distance sampling survey for birds on the water. It's called the snapshot method because birds in flight are recorded instantaneously at a regular interval. In some methods, the interval is such that birds are recorded in a 300 m x 300 m box every 300 m along the track line. You may find that your surveyors used something similar, or that your data can be thinned in a way that mimics this technique.

By the way, I note that your data set includes distances to birds detected in flight. It would be worth checking how these distances were estimated (using some sort of rangefinder or by eye?) because measuring distances to flying seabirds is notoriously difficult. Some analyses simply assume that birds in flight are detected perfectly within the 300 x 300 m snapshot box described above. This seems reasonable for large, conspicuous species. With this in mind, Dave Miller has been developing some extensions to the dsm() function that allow data with two detection functions (i.e. detection varies with distance for birds on the water and detection is perfect for birds in flight) to be treated in the same model. It might be worth contacting him if you're interested in density surface modelling with your data. If you're just looking for a design-based abundance estimate, I would suggest treating your on-water and in-flight separately, using a distance sampling analysis for the former and plot sampling analysis for the latter.

All the best,

Ewan

Hi Jeff,

Further to Eric's final comment, are you aware that seabirds at sea surveys often employ rather different methods to survey birds first detected on the water and those first detected in flight? Birds on the water generally move slowly with respect to the survey vessel, so they can readily be analysed in a distance sampling framework. In contrast, birds in flight, generally move faster than the vessel, violating one of the assumptions of distance sampling. In short, the motion of birds relative the survey vessel results in an increase in encounter rate. Tasker et al. proposed a 'snapshot' method to deal with this (but see Gaston, Auk, 104(2): 336-338 fro limitations). In effect, this is a plot survey for birds in flight, carried out simultaneously with the distance sampling survey for birds on the water. It's called the snapshot method because birds in flight are recorded instantaneously at a regular interval. In some methods, the interval is such that birds are recorded in a 300 m x 300 m box every 300 m along the track line. You may find that your surveyors used something similar, or that your data can be thinned in a way that mimics this technique.

By the way, I note that your data set includes distances to birds detected in flight. It would be worth checking how these distances were estimated (using some sort of rangefinder or by eye?) because measuring distances to flying seabirds is notoriously difficult. Some analyses simply assume that birds in flight are detected perfectly within the 300 x 300 m snapshot box described above. This seems reasonable for large, conspicuous species. With this in mind, Dave Miller has been developing some extensions to the dsm() function that allow data with two detection functions (i.e. detection varies with distance for birds on the water and detection is perfect for birds in flight) to be treated in the same model. It might be worth contacting him if you're interested in density surface modelling with your data. If you're just looking for a design-based abundance estimate, I would suggest treating your on-water and in-flight separately, using a distance sampling analysis for the former and plot sampling analysis for the latter.

All the best,

Ewan

Admittedly, the decision regarding that forward distance will be subjective, and open to dispute. Hi Deepti,

The error you're getting is likely related to an issue with the coordinate system being used.  I note that your function call is given an aftt_crs object, which I imagine was taken directly from the package vignette. This is unlikely to be appropriate for your study system, unless you are working in some area of the southeastern United States. I would recommend using a relevant CRS for your study area and seeing if that helps.

Please also check that the specified CRS matches the coordinate units in both the segments and prediction.grid objects. I was able to reproduce your error by having (x,y) coordinates in lat/lon format within the segments / prediction.grid data.frames, but using a mismatched (projected) coordinate system (e.g., with units of metres like in aftt_crs).

The warning messages that were returned in the console are intentional, and were built in to the package to make users aware of some of the things that are happening under the hood. In your case, the locations in prediction.grid are not regularly spaced (which is required to get a raster), so dsmextra automatically generates rasters based on the resolution you specify, and lets you know this is what it's done. Note that the resolution argument is typically a single number, so if you want a 200 x 200 m raster then you should only write resolution = 200.

The second warning is now deprecated in the latest version of the package (v 1.1.1) and should no longer appear. You might want to grab that version off Github as we've made a number of minor adjustments to functions throughout, in part to accompany the paper we recently wrote about the package (available here in pre-print form: https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/2041-210X.13469).

If you're still struggling after trying the above, I am happy to liaise with you off-list to solve the problem.
We can then report back to everyone with a solution.

Best

Hi group,

I am attempting to distance sample for wild sheep using time-lapse game cameras.  All cameras will simultaneously take pictures every 15 minutes, and I intend to put out measured marks (fence posts) in each camera view so that counts of animals can be pooled into distance bins.

My question is, would it be better to put the landmarks out linearly, (i.e. every 5 or 10 meters), or would it be better to place them out at distances that would make the area increase linearly?  One thing to note is that this situation is similar to point sampling, except that the area gained with increasing radius is not proportional to a gain in a full pi*r^2 , but pi*r^2*(42/360), because the field of view of the camera is only 42 degrees.

In my example, If I were to put out 8 landmarks, I can either put them out at distances 5-40 in 5m increments, or I can put them out so that area increases linearly which would make the spacing look more like (5.4, 8.1, 10.8, 13.6, 16.3, 19...etc).

Also, I could not find any suggestions for determining an adequate number of bins.  Is there a decision criterion for this?  Ideally I would like to minimize the number of bins perhaps maybe to 4, if feasible.

Best regards,

Interesting question.

Thinking about the placement of landmarks strictly from the perspective of fitting a detection function.  I believe the landmark posts will effectively become the cutpoints of the bins for the radial distances.  In this situation, I would suggest having a larger rather than a smaller number of bins; more like 8 bins rather than 4.  Remember this is the number of points of support you will have for assessing goodness of fit of your detection function model to data.

In addition, I would encourage you to perhaps have the landmarks more closely spaced near the cameras, with increasing separation at large distances; much like your suggestion of making landmark separation similar to distance band areas.  Having a number of landmark bands close to the camera gives the opportunity to closely examine the fit of the model to your data at the place where fit is most critical--namely close to distance zero.

Good day Pablo, and thanks Steve,

Additionally, in case it helps: Because the zone of potential detection is a sector, not a circle, randomizing sampling locations is insufficient to avoid bias in observed distances upon initial detection. Animals approaching the camera from in front of it contribute observations near the maximum range of the sensor, and observations closer to the camera, where detection probability as a function of distance is actually high, are missed. When animals approach from behind, we detect them at short distances (as expected), and miss them at longer distances, but we expect more misses at long distances with decreasing effectiveness of the sensor, so, on average, the bias in observed distances is positive. Figure 3.1 of my thesis https://research-repository.st-andrews.ac.uk/bitstream/handle/10023/18859/EricHowePhDThesis.pdf?sequence=3 (p 69 of the thesis, p 86 of the pdf document) attempts to illustrate the bias in distances observed upon initial detection.

We avoid the bias by recording distance observations at multiple points along the animals' path through the zone of potential detection (small t), so those observations at short distances aren't missed.

For comparison, Rowcliffe et al.'s (2008) Random Encounter Model accounted for the sector-shaped area sampled by "averaging across all possible angles of approach" (see their Figure 1), so they didn't ignore this potential source of bias, they just dealt with it differently.

Eric H
